title: The Strait of Hormuz: A Vital Waterway
summary: Why the narrow Strait of Hormuz, which links the Persian Gulf to the open sea, is one of the busiest and most important shipping routes on Earth.
poll: A narrow strip of water can matter more to world trade than a huge ocean.

versions.title: The Strait of Hormuz
versions.text:
Look at a map. Do you see a thin strip of water? It is a strait.

A strait is a narrow path of water. It joins two big seas.

This strait is very narrow. Land sits close on both sides. Ships must go slow and sail with care.

Many ships use it each day. Many carry oil. The oil goes out to the world.

So much oil goes through it. That makes it a busy sea path.

If ships could not use it, oil would be hard to move. Many lands would feel the change.

versions.title: The Strait of Hormuz: A Vital Waterway
versions.text:
A close look at a map of the Gulf region reveals a thin strip of water joining two seas, known as the Strait of Hormuz, named after a small island that once held a busy trading port many centuries ago.

A strait, in simple terms, is a narrow path of water that joins two larger seas together, letting ships travel between them without going around an entire landmass. The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the open sea beyond it, an area known as the Gulf of Oman. It also opens onto the wider Arabian Sea and, from there, the Indian Ocean.

At its narrowest point, the strait is not very wide at all, so large ships must stay within marked lanes as they pass through it. Land lies close on both sides of any vessel. So experienced captains must steer with great care throughout the crossing.

Every single day, a remarkable number of large ships travel through this narrow strait, and many of them carry crude oil loaded from ports inside the Persian Gulf, where some of the world's largest oil fields are found. That oil then continues on by sea to homes and factories in countries scattered around the world, often far away. Some of it also carries natural gas to the same distant places.

So much oil and natural gas pass through this one narrow strip of water that the strait has become one of the most important shipping routes on the planet. It is also one of the busiest waterways anywhere, a true chokepoint for the world's energy trade, and analysts call it strategically vital, given the sheer volume of oil extracted nearby and shipped by vessel each year.

Should ships ever be unable to safely use the strait, moving energy supplies out of the Gulf would become far more difficult and costly for every importing country. Many nations around the world would quickly feel the effects through rising energy prices.

A close examination of a map of the Gulf region reveals a thin strip of water joining two seas, known as the Strait of Hormuz, named after a small island that once held a busy trading port many centuries ago, long before modern tanker fleets existed in anything like their current form.

A strait, in simple terms, is a narrow passage of water that joins two larger seas together, letting vessels travel between them without going around an entire landmass. The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the open sea beyond it, an area known as the Gulf of Oman, which in turn opens onto the wider Arabian Sea and, eventually, the vast Indian Ocean.

At its narrowest point, the strait is not very wide at all, so large ships must stay within marked lanes as they navigate through it, since the depth available for genuinely safe passage is narrower still. Land lies close on both sides of any vessel, so experienced captains must steer with great care throughout every moment of the crossing, particularly where the lanes bend.

Every single day, a remarkable volume of large ships travels through this narrow strait, and much of it carries crude oil loaded from ports inside the Persian Gulf, where some of the world's largest oil fields are concentrated close to the shore. That oil then continues on by sea to homes and factories in countries scattered around the world, often thousands of kilometers from where it was extracted.

So much oil and natural gas pass through this one narrow strip of water that the strait has become one of the most economically important shipping routes on the planet. It is a true chokepoint, and energy analysts routinely call it strategically vital, given the sheer volume of oil extracted nearby and shipped onward by vessel each year.

Should ships ever be unable to safely use the strait, moving energy supplies out of the Gulf would become far more difficult and costly for every importing country, since pipeline routes can realistically carry only a small share of the total volume that normally moves by sea. Many nations around the world would quickly feel the effects through rising energy prices and a noticeably tighter overall supply.

versions.title: The Strait of Hormuz: A Vital Waterway
versions.text:
A close examination of a map of the Gulf region reveals a remarkably thin strip of water joining two seas, known as the Strait of Hormuz, named after a small island that once held a busy trading port many centuries ago, long before modern tanker fleets existed in anything resembling their current form.

A strait, in strict geographic terms, is a narrow passage of water that joins two larger bodies of water together, allowing vessels to travel between them without circling an entire landmass. The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the open sea beyond it, an area known as the Gulf of Oman, which in turn opens onto the wider Arabian Sea and, eventually, the vast expanse of the Indian Ocean.

At its narrowest point, the strait measures only a few dozen kilometers across, and large oceangoing ships must remain within carefully marked shipping lanes as they navigate through it, since the depth available for genuinely safe passage is considerably narrower still. Land lies close on both sides of any vessel that travels there, so experienced captains must steer with great care throughout every moment of the crossing, particularly where the lanes curve sharply around the coastline.

Every single day, a remarkable volume of large tanker traffic moves through this narrow strait, much of it carrying crude oil loaded from ports situated inside the Persian Gulf, where some of the world's largest and most productive oil fields are concentrated close to the shoreline. That oil then continues on by sea to refineries, homes, and factories in countries scattered across the globe, frequently thousands of kilometers from where it was originally extracted.

So much oil and natural gas pass through this single narrow strip of water that the Strait of Hormuz has become one of the most economically significant shipping routes on the entire planet. It constitutes a genuine chokepoint, and energy analysts routinely characterize it as strategically vital, given the sheer volume of crude extracted nearby and conveyed onward by vessel every single year.

Should oceangoing ships ever be unable to safely use the strait, moving energy supplies out of the Gulf would become far more difficult and costly for every importing country, since alternative pipeline routes can realistically carry only a small fraction of the total volume that normally passes by sea. Many nations around the world would quickly feel the effects through rising energy prices and a noticeably tighter overall supply chain.

versions.title: The Strait of Hormuz: A Vital Waterway
versions.text:
A close examination of a map of the Gulf region reveals a remarkably thin strip of water joining two seas, designated the Strait of Hormuz, a name derived from a small island that once held a prominent trading port many centuries ago, long before modern tanker fleets existed in anything resembling their current form.

A strait, in strict geographic terminology, constitutes a narrow passage of water joining two larger bodies of water together, thereby allowing vessels to travel between them without circumnavigating an entire landmass in order to do so. The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf to the open sea beyond it, a region designated the Gulf of Oman, which in turn opens onto the wider Arabian Sea and, eventually, the vast expanse of the Indian Ocean.

At its narrowest point, the strait measures merely a few dozen kilometers across, and large oceangoing vessels must remain within carefully demarcated shipping lanes as they navigate through it, since the depth available for genuinely safe passage is considerably narrower still. Land lies in close proximity on both sides of any vessel that travels there, so experienced captains must steer with exceptional care throughout every moment of the crossing, particularly where the lanes curve sharply around the surrounding coastline.

Every single day, a remarkable volume of large tanker traffic transits this narrow strait, much of it conveying crude oil loaded from ports situated inside the Persian Gulf, where some of the world's largest and most productive oil fields are concentrated close to the shoreline. That oil subsequently continues on by sea to refineries, households, and factories in countries scattered across the globe, frequently thousands of kilometers from where it was originally extracted from beneath the ground.

So substantial is the volume of oil and natural gas passing through this single narrow strip of water that the Strait of Hormuz has become one of the most economically significant shipping routes on the entire planet. It constitutes a genuine chokepoint, and energy analysts routinely characterize it as strategically vital, given the sheer volume of crude extracted nearby and conveyed onward by vessel every single year.

Should oceangoing vessels ever be rendered unable to safely use the strait, moving energy supplies out of the Gulf would become far more difficult and costly for every importing nation, since alternative pipeline routes can realistically convey only a small fraction of the total volume that normally transits by sea. Numerous nations around the world would rapidly feel the effects through rising energy prices and a noticeably constrained overall supply chain for years to come.

HIGH.prompt: Explain why a narrow strait can matter more to the global economy than its small size might suggest. Use at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained why the strait's importance outweighs its small size.
I used at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I used at least two key words, such as chokepoint or volume.
HIGH.modelAnswer: A narrow strait like Hormuz can matter more to the global economy than its small size suggests because so much of the world's seaborne energy trade is forced to pass through that one chokepoint each day. The article explains that some of the world's largest oil fields sit close to the Persian Gulf's shoreline, and the crude oil extracted there has no practical way to reach the rest of the world except by vessel through this narrow passage, since alternative overland pipelines can carry only a small fraction of that total volume. Because the strait concentrates such an enormous share of global energy shipping into a passage only a few dozen kilometers wide, its narrow geography gives it an economic importance far out of proportion to its modest physical size.
